331.event: In the 1630s prices for rare tulip bulbs in Holland rose to extraordinary heights, and ordinary families were drawn into buying bulbs for resale, with bulbs sold and resold many times without ever leaving the ground. Early in 1637 doubts arose as to whether prices would keep rising, and the price structure collapsed almost overnight, ruining many who had bought at the top. Historians still debate how widespread the damage was, but the boom and sudden crash of early 1637 are well documented.
331.explanation: Buyers acted as if the high value of a flower bulb was a lasting fact rather than a passing mood of the market. The episode became one of history's best-known warnings about treating a temporary condition as permanent.
331.tie_back: Valluvar calls it the lowest folly to take what cannot last as if it will endure, which is exactly the mistake the tulip buyers made about bulb prices.
331._accuracy_note: A strong, well-known illustration of mistaking the fleeting for the permanent, though it concerns market prices rather than life itself, and modern scholars think the scale of ruin was smaller than the popular story claims.

332.event: The Scottish financier John Law founded a note-issuing bank in Paris and merged it with the company holding France's trading rights in the Mississippi Valley; as controller general of finances in 1720 he presided over intense speculation that drove the company's shares from about 500 livres to many times that value. In the summer of 1720, as shareholders rushed to turn their paper into gold and silver, share prices collapsed and the bank notes lost their value. Law, politically isolated, left France in December 1720.
332.explanation: Fortunes built up over months of speculation vanished within weeks once the crowd of investors turned and left together. The crash destroyed public confidence in paper money and companies in France for a generation.
332.tie_back: The kural compares great wealth to a theatre crowd that gathers gradually and scatters all at once when the show ends, just as the Mississippi investors poured in and then fled together.
332._accuracy_note: Closely matches the image of wealth that assembles slowly around a spectacle and disperses suddenly, though the kural speaks of wealth in general rather than a speculative bubble.

333.event_title: Jamsetji Tata endows half his fortune for the Indian Institute of Science
333.event: In 1898 the industrialist Jamsetji Tata set aside 14 buildings and four landed properties in Bombay, worth about 30 lakh rupees and roughly half his wealth, as an endowment for a research university of science. He kept the offer open through years of negotiation with the colonial government and reaffirmed it in a codicil to his will shortly before he died in 1904. The Indian Institute of Science was established in Bangalore by a vesting order in 1909 and admitted its first students in 1911.
333.explanation: Tata turned a large part of a fortune that could have been lost or spent into an institution that has trained generations of Indian scientists. The gift has outlasted him by more than a century.
333.tie_back: Valluvar says that since wealth does not stay, one should at once turn it into deeds that do stay, and Tata converted half his fortune into a lasting institution of learning.
333._accuracy_note: Almost a dramatisation of exchanging perishable wealth for an enduring good, though the gift took years to bear fruit rather than being spent at once.

334.event_title: Steve Jobs's Stanford commencement address on mortality
334.event: Apple co-founder Steve Jobs gave the commencement address at Stanford University and devoted the third of his three stories to death. He told the graduates that for 33 years he had looked in the mirror each morning and asked whether he would want to do what he was about to do if it were the last day of his life, and that when the answer was no for too many days in a row he knew he needed to change something. He described a recent brush with a serious illness and urged them not to waste their limited time.
334.explanation: The speech became one of the most widely shared commencement addresses because it treated each ordinary day as a measured part of a limited life. It shows a practical habit of noticing that every day spent is a day used up.
334.tie_back: The kural says the day only looks like a harmless unit of time, while the wise see it as a saw cutting away at life, and Jobs described a daily practice built on exactly that awareness.
334._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of the wise person who sees each passing day as a cut into life, though the speech's emphasis is on choosing well rather than on the wearing-away image itself.

335.event_title: Thomas Guy builds Guy's Hospital in the last years of his life
335.event: Thomas Guy, a London bookseller and governor of St Thomas' Hospital who had grown very rich by selling his South Sea Company shares in 1720, decided in 1721, at about the age of 76, to build a new hospital for patients who could not be helped elsewhere. Construction began in 1722, and the building was roofed before he died on 27 December 1724. His will left most of his remaining fortune, over 200,000 pounds, to complete and maintain the hospital, which opened soon after his death.
335.explanation: Guy did not postpone his great charity to a distant future but began it in old age and pushed it forward while he still could. Guy's Hospital remains one of London's major teaching hospitals.
335.tie_back: Valluvar urges people to hurry and do good before the tongue is stilled at death, and Guy raced to build his hospital in the final years of his life.
335._accuracy_note: A strong fit for doing good urgently before death arrives, though the sources do not record Guy describing his haste in these terms.

336.event_title: The eruption of Vesuvius buries Pompeii
336.event: In 79 CE Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the thriving Roman town of Pompeii under a deep layer of volcanic ash and pumice, while nearby Herculaneum disappeared under volcanic flows. Busy towns full of people, shops and homes were lost in a single eruption. The buried ruins were rediscovered centuries later and now give a detailed picture of Roman daily life frozen at one moment.
336.explanation: Pompeii has become the classic image of how suddenly ordinary life can vanish. Its preserved streets show a world that was going about its business one day and gone the next.
336.tie_back: The kural's ironic 'greatness' of the world is that one who was here yesterday is gone today, and Pompeii shows a whole town undergoing that change in a single day.
336._accuracy_note: A vivid illustration of the yesterday-here, today-gone suddenness the kural describes, though it is a mass disaster rather than the ordinary death of an individual.

337.event_title: Antoni Gaudi dies with the Sagrada Familia unfinished
337.event: The architect Antoni Gaudi, who had devoted more than four decades to designing and building the Sagrada Familia basilica, was struck by a tram in Barcelona on 7 June 1926 while walking to church. He died at the Hospital de la Santa Creu on 10 June and was buried in the crypt of the basilica. The building, planned to take generations, was still far from complete and construction continued long after his death.
337.explanation: Gaudi's vast, long-range design stands in sharp contrast to the sudden, ordinary accident that ended his life. His plans outlived him by a century, carried on by others.
337.tie_back: Valluvar remarks that people who cannot be sure of the next moment still carry countless plans, and Gaudi's enormous project was cut short in an instant by a passing tram.
337._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of vast plans meeting sudden uncertainty, though Gaudi knowingly planned for others to finish the work, so it is not a portrait of foolish overplanning.

338.event_title: Benjamin Franklin writes his own mock epitaph
338.event: As a young printer of about 22, Benjamin Franklin wrote a humorous epitaph for himself, describing his body in the grave as the cover of an old book whose contents had been torn out and whose lettering and gilding had been stripped away. He added that the work itself would not be lost but would appear again in a new and better edition. Several autograph copies survive, and in his will he asked for a simple inscription on his actual gravestone instead.
338.explanation: Franklin's famous image treats the body as an outer case that is left empty once its real contents depart. It became one of the best-known epitaphs in American literature.
338.tie_back: The kural compares body and life to an egg or nest left empty and alone when the bird flies off, and Franklin pictured his own body as an empty book cover left behind.
338._accuracy_note: A close parallel to the image of an emptied container left behind, though it is a witty literary piece rather than an event of departure itself.

339.event_title: Socrates compares death to a dreamless sleep at his trial
339.event: In 399 BCE an Athenian jury found the philosopher Socrates guilty and sentenced him to death. In Plato's account of his defence speech, the Apology, Socrates told the jurors that death must be either a dreamless sleep, which he would count as a gain, or a migration of the soul to another place, which would be even better. He therefore argued that death was not something to be feared.
339.explanation: The speech is one of the founding texts of Western philosophy's reflection on death, and it uses the familiar experience of deep sleep to make death less frightening.
339.tie_back: Valluvar likens death to falling asleep and birth to waking, and Socrates, facing execution, likewise reasoned about death through the image of sleep and a passage to another life.
339._accuracy_note: A strong parallel for death as sleep, though Socrates left open whether anything follows, whereas the kural pairs sleep with waking into a new birth.

340.event_title: Basho sells his home and sets out on the Narrow Road to the Deep North
340.event: In 1689 the haiku poet Matsuo Basho sold his home outside Edo and set out on foot, with a companion, on a journey of about five months through the remote northern provinces of Japan. He recorded the journey in prose and haiku in Oku no Hosomichi (The Narrow Road to the Deep North), published in 1694. Basho died in 1694 while on another journey.
340.explanation: Basho chose to live as a lifelong traveller without a fixed home, and his travel diary became a classic of Japanese literature. His life embodies the idea of existence as a passage rather than a settled dwelling.
340.tie_back: The kural pictures the soul as a lodger in a borrowed corner that has not yet found its permanent home, and Basho gave up his own house to live as a wanderer between temporary lodgings.
340._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit: Basho's homeless wandering mirrors the image of a temporary lodger, but the kural is about the soul and the body, not about travel.
